title: Spoofing
text: Spoofing is placing orders you intend to cancel before they trade, to move the price toward an order you do want filled. In US futures, it has been a named offence since 2010.

title: Why it matters
text: The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 added it to the Commodity Exchange Act, in section 4c(a)(5)(C). The words are short: bidding or offering with the intent to cancel the bid or offer before execution. The key word is intent. Cancelling is normal; cancelling as a plan is the offence. And the penalties are large.

title: How layering works
text: Here is the pattern. A trader wants to sell 10 contracts, and rests an offer just above the market. Then they place large bids at several price levels below, a layer of fake demand. Other traders see the bigger bid side and lift their prices. The small offer fills at the better price. Within moments, the large bids are cancelled, often before anyone can trade against them. Then it may run again on the other side.

title: Enforcement
text: The first federal criminal case under the new law was Michael Coscia. Using two algorithms, he made nearly $1.4 million in less than three months in 2011. A jury convicted him on 3 November 2015, and he was sentenced to three years in prison. In September 2020, JPMorgan agreed to pay $920 million to settle spoofing in precious metals and Treasury futures, from 2008 to 2016. The CFTC called it the largest monetary relief it had ever imposed.

title: Surveillance
text: Surveillance looks for the footprint. Large orders that are cancelled soon after they are placed. Fills that keep landing on the other side. Cancels that cluster right after a fill. Order-to-trade ratios far above a trader's normal. In the EU, RTS 6 makes trading firms run their own surveillance, with alerts by the start of the next trading day. An alert is a question, not a verdict.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's ITCH feed carries every add, cancel and execution, by order reference number, and the drop copy links each fill to its order. That is the raw material for a self-surveillance check: order lifetimes, cancel ratios, and which side each fill was on. Run it on the lab's market maker and it cancels constantly, because it moves its quotes with the market. A ratio alone cannot tell quoting from spoofing.

title: Takeaway
text: So what do pros do? They make sure every order they send is meant to trade. They document why each strategy cancels when it does. They run surveillance on themselves, and keep complete order logs. And they treat an unexplained pattern as a problem to fix today. This is education, not legal advice.
